fatal_errors: The material system is Q235 steel rather than the target uncoated SS316L substrate.

The proposed electroplated 1–25 µm chromium-rich coating does not reconstruct the approximately 150 µm atmospheric-plasma-sprayed AlCoCrFeNi high-entropy-alloy coating or its post-deposition annealing.
The exposure conditions differ fundamentally: 3.5% NaCl at 20–60 °C replaces 3.5 wt% H2SO4 electrochemistry and 900 °C cyclic molten-salt hot corrosion.

Chromium-rich plating is described as providing cathodic protection, although chromium is generally more noble than carbon steel and coating defects can instead promote galvanic attack of exposed Q235; barrier/passivation is the more defensible mechanism.
The asserted optimum thickness of 10–15 µm has no cited evidence or mechanistic derivation.
The experiment measures only generic corrosion rate and resistance and therefore cannot isolate oxide passivation, barrier integrity, galvanic coupling, or coating porosity as the governing cause.
explanation: The hypothesis shares only the broad idea that a chromium-containing protective layer may form an oxide barrier and lower corrosion relative to an untreated metal. It otherwise misses the target material, HEA composition, plasma-spray process, coating thickness, 550 °C annealing optimum, microstructural mediators, acidic electrochemical environment, and 900 °C molten-salt exposures. The untreated control and thickness series provide a rudimentary test, but mediator-sensitive measurements such as electrochemical impedance, polarization, coating-defect characterization, XRD/XPS, SEM/EDS, and post-exposure cross-sections are absent. A stronger falsification study would also compare intact and deliberately defected coatings and measure galvanic currents; acceleration localized at defects would directly contradict the claimed cathodic-protection mechanism. With no supporting evidence and a likely incorrect electrochemical mechanism, this is not a well-supported alternative.
